Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

could you help me get the listening afternoon in the back room at Juniper Street Books and Records into better shape? i have been collecting vinyl for about twelve years, and the room is small enough that it feels welcoming, but also small enough that people, coats, and record sleeves can get in each other's way. i am hoping for eight or ten people on a sunday in late april, probably from two until four, though i have not checked whether the room is free on the 21st or the 28th. i want it to feel like a friendly chance to listen together, not a sales event or a lecture about having the right equipment.

most of my records are in two low shelves at home, and i have a smaller box of things i bring to swaps. i started making a list last winter, but the notes are in three places: a spreadsheet, a notebook with a blue cover, and labels on the dividers. the spreadsheet has artist, title, year if i can confirm it, and a note about condition, but i did not finish the last two shelves. some of the handwritten notes are more personal than useful, like “played this during the storm,” and i am not sure whether those belong in a public list. i would appreciate your eye on how much information people need before they hear something.

for the afternoon, i thought we could play a few short sides and talk about why we keep the records we keep. i have a small Audio-Technica turntable, a receiver that sometimes needs the volume knob nudged, and two compact speakers. they are fine for the room, i think, but i have not tested them with more than four people listening at once. the shop has folding chairs, though there are only six, and the narrow table by the window might hold the sleeves we choose. if you have time, could you help me work out where people can stand without blocking the door or the path to the counter?

these are the practical bits i have written down so far, and some of them may need changing once we see the room:
1. check with Jo, who manages the shop, whether the 21st or 28th is available, and whether the back-room door should stay open during the event.
2. ask if we can borrow four more chairs from the upstairs office; i think there are some there, but i have not asked Jo yet.
3. bring a power strip and painter's tape, because the outlet is near the bookcase and i do not want a cable across the walking space.
4. decide whether people should bring one record to share or just come and listen; i am leaning toward no requirement, so nobody has to carry a valuable sleeve on the bus.
5. put a small sign by the front counter, but keep the wording simple and make clear that people can come in without knowing anything about turntables.

for the records, i was thinking of bringing “Blue Train” by John Coltrane, my copy of “Songs in the Key of Life,” and a 1982 pressing of “Nebraska.” the Coltrane album has a little surface noise between tracks, but the music itself plays through, and the Stevie Wonder sleeve has a crease at the lower right corner. i have two different copies of “Nebraska,” and the one i would bring is the quieter one, not necessarily the more collectible copy. i could also bring a local compilation called “North End After Dark,” which was made by the college radio station in 1996. its track list is handwritten inside, and one song is credited only as “The Visitors.” i do not know who that band was, so i would rather say that plainly than guess in front of people.

there are other records i might include, but i do not want to make the choices sound like a ranking. my copy of “Hounds of Love” is an ordinary reissue, and it still matters to me because my aunt played it while we cooked on saturday mornings. a Miles Davis record from a flea market has a pencilled price of four dollars on the inner sleeve, which i have left there. i also have a seven-inch single from the neighborhood band Glass Orchard, bought at their show at the Lantern Room in 2011. the label has a phone number printed on it, but it might no longer be current. those details are part of how i remember finding the records, though i do not need to tell the whole story for every one.

could you help me choose a sensible order that gives people a bit of variety without making the afternoon feel overplanned? i was thinking we could begin with something familiar, then play the radio compilation, and finish with one side that is slower and quieter. that is only a possible order, because the room might get noisy when customers come through the shop, and i do not want anyone to feel they have to sit silently. i would like space for people to ask about pressing differences, thrift-store finds, and how to clean a record safely, but i am not trying to give technical advice beyond what i actually know. i use a carbon-fiber brush before playing, and for dusty records i use a manual washer with distilled water.

one concern is handling: i can put the records in clean outer sleeves, but i want to ask people to hold them by the edges and avoid touching the grooves without sounding fussy. Jo once said, “people relax when they can see what is happening,” and that seems right to me, so maybe the turntable should be on the wider end of the table, where it is visible but not within easy reach of every passing sleeve. i would also like to have a few plain paper inner sleeves available in case one of mine splits, though i have not counted how many are left in the drawer.

if you can look over the plan with me and help check the room, the chair count, and the order of records, that would be great. i can bring the spreadsheet and notebook so we can compare them, but i do not want to spend the whole afternoon correcting my catalog instead of preparing for the event. please tell me if the plan seems too crowded for a two-hour visit, or if there is one practical detail i have missed; i am still unsure about the date, and i do not want to announce it until Jo confirms the room.", "output": "Could you help me get the listening afternoon in the back room at Juniper Street Books and Records into better shape?
